strengths: Combining Fourier neural operators, adversarially generated measure pairs, and short Sinkhorn bootstrapping is a coherent contribution to amortized OT computation. Generalization across datasets and grid resolutions is a useful objective beyond solving individual transport problems.

The empirical warm-start results are promising. Across 500 evaluation samples, Table 1 reports substantial iteration reductions, while Table 2 shows approximately 2.75–3.4× speedups on the 64×64 datasets. The appendix strengthens this evidence with resolution sweeps, variable-regularization experiments, and marginal-feasibility curves.

Predicting dual potentials allows subsequent refinement with standard Sinkhorn iterations. Proposition 5 provides a useful residual-to-solution error bound for positive kernels and consistently centered potentials.

The manuscript supplies architecture and training details, a computational budget, and a code-and-weights link. It also acknowledges limitations concerning fixed costs and extrapolation to higher resolutions.
weaknesses: The principal generator-universality claim is not established for the implemented method. Appendix C explicitly uses unequal latent/output dimensions and does not enforce the required Lipschitz constraint. Furthermore, Corollary 4 is false as stated: in one dimension, G1(x)=ReLU(x/2+1) and G2(z)=ReLU(z/2) satisfy the assumptions, but G1(G2(z))≥1, so their composition cannot generate values in (0,1). Theorem 3 also treats a ReLU map as invertible without handling its boundary atoms. These issues require correcting the theoretical statements and narrowing claims about the trained generator.

The OT formulations and predicted potentials need reconciliation. Equation (1) uses a negative KL penalty, apparently a sign error, whereas Algorithm 1 labels the transport-only quantity ⟨C,Π⟩ as the regularized objective. Additionally, the potentials associated with the μ⊗ν reference measure in Equation (3) differ from the logarithms of the scaling vectors in Algorithm 1 by marginal-dependent shifts. Consequently, Proposition 2 does not directly justify convergence of the actual learning targets as currently presented. These distinctions matter for interpreting both the theoretical motivation and reported errors.

The comparisons do not adequately establish superiority over existing learned initialization methods or explain which proposed components drive performance. Meta OT is excluded based on an asserted out-of-distribution weakness rather than directly evaluated at compatible resolutions. Controlled comparisons against nonadversarial generation and dual-objective training are also missing. Gaussian initialization is omitted from runtime comparisons because of implementation difficulties, and timings from other papers cannot substitute for a matched comparison. Table 2 additionally shows a slowdown on MNIST.

The geometry experiments have both methodological and evidential gaps. Algorithm 3 applies softmax directly to probability weights; this is not a simplex projection and changes a nonuniform optimum even when its gradient is zero. Appendix A.4's derivative of the outer Sinkhorn divergence also omits the derivative of its source self-interaction term. These formulas need correction or clarification against the implementation. The selected barycenter and geodesic images are encouraging, but quantitative errors over multiple examples and a reproducible GeONet evaluation are needed to support the claimed geometric accuracy and significant superiority.

Proposition 5 supports a narrower conclusion than the repeated claim that minimizing the bootstrapping loss provably minimizes ground-truth loss. Its bound implies that a vanishing residual gives vanishing solution error for fixed problem parameters; it does not establish monotonic improvement of ground-truth error or convergence of the detached-target adversarial training procedure. The contraction-based constant can also become extremely loose at small regularization.

The practical accuracy claims should distinguish transport-cost agreement, marginal feasibility, and plan accuracy. Figure 14 usefully reports marginal violations, but the headline runtime comparisons stop at 1% transport-cost error rather than a joint feasibility and optimality criterion. More precise accuracy-versus-time evaluation is needed before extending the demonstrated cost-prediction benefits to reliable transport-plan computation.
